name: transaction-script
intent: Organizes the business logic of a single request as one procedure - read the data it needs, validate and calculate, write the results and complete in one database transaction - trading object-model structure for a straight-line implementation that can be read top to bottom.
problem: A request-scoped use case (book a room, place an order, recognize revenue, import a file) has to be implemented, and its logic mixes input validation, calculation and persistence. Modelling the domain as objects may be premature, or the team may not be ready for it, yet the implementation still needs each request's steps to stay visible and its transaction boundary to be explicit.
context: Applies where business logic is simple to moderately complex, where the system is naturally described as a series of transactions each driven by one request (HTTP handler, CLI command, queue message, batch job), and where a thin data-source gateway or the database itself is the persistence seam. Also the right starting point under delivery pressure or for a team new to domain modelling - provided the growth path to a Domain Model is watched deliberately.
benefits: Simplicity above all: the whole use case is one procedure, readable from the request data to the commit, with essentially no framework or model machinery in between.
Very little performance overhead: the script talks to the database directly or through a thin gateway, so no mapping, identity or unit-of-work layer sits between the logic and SQL.
The transaction boundary is obvious and testable by inspection - one script, one database transaction, begun at the start and committed at the end.
Fast delivery for small logic: a new use case is a new procedure, so features land without first designing an object model or negotiating with the rest of the domain layer.
Pairs naturally with simple data-source patterns (Table Data Gateway, Row Data Gateway) and with stored procedures that already do part of the work.

Keeps presentation out of the domain logic only as far as the team insists - scripts that take plain parameters and return data are easy to call from several entry points and to cover with a test database.
tradeoffs: Duplication between scripts: because each script is written in isolation, shared rules get copied instead of shared, and the copies drift as the requirements change.

Structure collapses as logic grows: validation, pricing and eligibility rules that belong together end up scattered across unrelated procedures, so line-by-line readability hides policy inconsistency.

The cutover is expensive: refactoring a Transaction Script design into a Domain Model is a large, cross-cutting change, so the decision has to be revisited early rather than when the tangle is already deep.
Logic entangled with SQL and connection handling makes rule-level unit tests awkward - testing a validation usually needs a database or a carefully introduced gateway seam.

Discipline required to keep presentation out: once a script parses HTTP or renders output it becomes untestable, and Fowler's advice not to call presentation logic from scripts is violated in practice more often than not.
No shared vocabulary for invariants: the database constraints become the only enforcement point, and the same invariant gets re-checked inconsistently in different scripts.

participants.responsibility: The procedure that implements exactly one request end to end: takes plain input, validates, calculates, reads and writes through the gateway, and completes (commits) the transaction.
The class or module the scripts live in - usually one subject-area class holding several related scripts, or one class per script when scripts must be handled as objects (Command style).
A factored-out common subtask shared by several scripts, kept free of presentation concerns and callable from any script that needs it.

The thin wrapper (table/row data gateway or raw SQL helper) through which the script reaches the database; it accepts the caller's transaction or connection handle so the script keeps control of atomicity.
The explicit begin/commit/rollback around a single script invocation that makes the request atomic - normally the one database transaction the pattern is named after.
The presentation-layer caller (controller, endpoint handler, job runner) that passes request data into the script and renders or returns its result; it contains no business logic itself.

use_cases: Booking a hotel room: check availability, calculate the rate, insert the booking and confirm - one request, one transaction.
Revenue recognition (Fowler's example): given a contract and an as-of date, calculate the recognitions and persist them, or report the revenue already recognized.
CRUD write endpoints in a simple admin or back-office application where each screen maps to one operation.
Batch and integration jobs: import a file, validate rows, write the accepted rows and report the rejects in one transaction per batch.
Queue or message handlers that carry out one command (place order, cancel subscription, refund payment) and acknowledge only after commit.
Reporting and ETL steps that read a slice of data, transform it and write results, where the logic is genuinely a straight line of steps.

Django request-atomicity: with ATOMIC_REQUESTS enabled (or @transaction.atomic on the view), the whole view function is the script - Django begins the transaction at request start, commits on a successful response and rolls back on exception, exactly the one-script-one-transaction shape.

Laravel request handlers that wrap the validate-calculate-persist sequence in a DB::transaction closure: the closure commits when it returns and rolls back automatically if it throws, so the closure body is the script and its extent is the boundary.

Spring @Transactional service methods: an AOP proxy begins the transaction before the method and commits after it returns, making each annotated method a Transaction Script whose signature is the request and whose boundary is declarative.
avoid_when: Business rules are complex, interlocking or fast-changing: use a Domain Model and put behaviour with the data it protects.
The logic is one set-oriented pass over whole tables or record sets (bulk updates, aggregations over a result set): Table Module expresses that shape directly.
Several callers (UI, batch, integration) need one coherent boundary of operations and transaction ownership: introduce a Service Layer and let it host the scripts.
Invariants must hold across a cluster of objects or modules: an Aggregate (or Specification for reusable rules) makes those rules explicit and enforceable in one place.
The 'script' would be a 300-line procedure touching five systems: that is not simplicity, and the honest step is to split the logic or model it.
anti_patterns: Fat script: a 300-line procedure that parses the request, validates, prices, writes SQL, sends e-mail and formats the response - the honest procedure has become a dumping ground.
Copy-paste rules: the same eligibility or pricing rule reimplemented in several scripts, drifting apart because nothing owns it.
Hidden transaction: relying on per-statement auto-commit for a multi-step write, so a failure leaves the request half applied.
Script that renders: building the HTML/serialization inside the script, which makes the business logic untestable without the full presentation stack.
God service class: grouping unrelated subject areas into one class so their scripts share mutable fields and start depending on each other's half-finished state.
Business logic split between scripts and stored procedures, with neither side owning the rule and both applying it differently.
design_principles: Keep each request's logic in one procedure with one obvious transaction boundary - atomicity by construction, not by accident.
Separation of concerns: presentation stays out of the script, and persistence stays behind a thin gateway.
Do not repeat yourself: the second occurrence of a subtask is the moment to factor it into a shared subprocedure.
Simplicity first, but honest about growth - the pattern is a starting point, not a life sentence; revisit it when duplication or rule complexity becomes structural.
Explicit over implicit: transaction control, validation at the edge and error handling are written out, not hidden in framework magic the reader cannot see.
best_practices: Write one script per request/use case and name it after the operation, not after the tables it touches; group related scripts in a subject-area class or module.
Take plain parameters (or a command object) in and return data out - never the HTTP request, never the response object.
Wrap every script in exactly one transaction: begin before the first read that drives a decision, commit once, and roll back on every error path (including the ones you think cannot happen).
Keep SQL behind a thin data-source gateway that accepts the connection or transaction handle, so the script owns atomicity and can be tested against a scratch database.
Factor repeated subtasks into subprocedures (or a shared Specification) at the second occurrence rather than copying them.
Validate input at the script edge and let database constraints enforce the invariants that must hold regardless of which script runs.
Review the decision regularly: when rules multiply, duplicate or need to be explained to the business, extract a Domain Model early - the later the cutover, the more expensive it is.
sources: Martin Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (Addison-Wesley, 2003) - Transaction Script, Domain Logic Patterns, Chapter 9 (How It Works / When to Use It, pp. 110-112).
